input.title: fix: reject cross-realm FormData request bodies
input.description:
## This relates to...

Fixes #5520. Related context: #5500 / #5502 (legacy dispatcher bridge), #5016 and #4285 (fetch-side cross-realm FormData behavior, unchanged here).

## Rationale

`request()` accepts FormData bodies through the duck-typed `util.isFormDataLike()` check, but only undici's own `FormData` can be encoded: the multipart extraction is gated on the `webidl.is.FormData` brand check. A FormData from another realm (Node.js' builtin `globalThis.FormData`, another undici copy, a polyfill) passed the gate, fell through the extraction, and was dispatched as a body that never produced any bytes: the request hung silently until an external timeout, with zero bytes written to the socket (full version matrix and reproductions in #5520).

Per review direction (encode vs reject, maintainers chose reject): such bodies now fail fast with `InvalidArgumentError`. The check lives in the `Request` constructor, where other invalid body types are already rejected, so both the HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 clients reject cleanly at dispatch time and the fetch code is untouched. The FormData brand check is loaded lazily so the fetch machinery is not pulled in upfront.

Note for changelog purposes: this is a behavior change relative to v6, which encoded cross-realm FormData successfully (v7.0.0 through 7.19.x failed these bodies with an unrelated TypeError; 7.20.0+ hung).

## Changes

- `lib/core/request.js`: FormData-like bodies that are not instances of undici's `FormData` now throw `InvalidArgumentError` instead of falling through to iterable handling.
- `test/issue-5520.js`: cross-realm FormData rejection over HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (own-FormData encoding is already covered by `test/client-request.js` and `test/http2-body.js`).

### Features

N/A

### Bug Fixes

- `request()` with a FormData from another realm now rejects immediately with a clear error instead of hanging forever.

### Breaking Changes and Deprecations

N/A (the affected input previously hung or produced a broken body; it never worked on v7/v8)

- [x] Documented (behavior fix; error message self-describes)
- [x] Review ready
- [ ] In review
- [ ] Merge ready

Make `extractBody`'s FormData branch accept what `isFormDataLike` accepts: the multipart encoder already only uses the public entry iterator (`for (const [name, value] of object)`) and Blob duck-typing (`name`, `type`, `size`, `stream()`), so encoding a foreign FormData should produce identical output. (The private `#boundary` getter is the only own-state dependency and can fall back to generating a boundary locally.)

3. Independently: reconsider the eager legacy-symbol claim at require time (as proposed in #5500), since it converts every intra-copy strictness change into a cross-copy breakage for code that never imports the new version.

Happy to turn either fix direction into a PR.

input.description:
## Summary

Addresses #23451: build.rolldownOptions.preserveEntrySignatures shows incorrect default

## Changed files

- `docs/config/build-options.md`

## Validation

- `git diff --check`: passed

Fixes #23451
input.taskText:
### Documentation is

- [ ] Missing
- [ ] Outdated
- [x] Confusing
- [ ] Not sure?

### Explain in Detail

`build.rolldownOptions.preserveEntrySignatures` is documented by the underlying Rolldown type with a default value of `'exports-only'`.

However, Vite overrides this value internally depending on the build mode. For a regular client build, Vite sets it to `false`:

```ts
preserveEntrySignatures: ssr
  ? 'allow-extension'
  : libOptions
    ? 'strict'
    : false
```

This means that leaving `build.rolldownOptions.preserveEntrySignatures` undefined in a regular Vite build does not behave as the documented Rolldown default (`'exports-only'`), but as `false`.

This was confusing in my case because I have multiple TypeScript entry points whose exports are consumed as ES modules from a Blazor application. I expected the documented default to preserve those exports, but I need to explicitly set:

```ts
build: {
  rolldownOptions: {
    preserveEntrySignatures: 'exports-only',
  },
}
```

I understand that `build.rolldownOptions` is merged with Vite's internal Rolldown options, but it isn't clear that Vite overrides this particular default.

Relevant code:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/5bce8ca0f19bfdd5206c98bfabc1f8453deb32c7/packages/vite/src/node/build.ts#L658-L662

### Your Suggestion for Changes

Document the effective Vite defaults for `preserveEntrySignatures`, or otherwise mention that Vite overrides Rolldown's default.

For example:

* regular client build: `false`
* library build: `'strict'`
* SSR/server build: `'allow-extension'`

It may also be worth considering the IntelliSense/JSDoc experience, since the exposed `RolldownOptions` type reports Rolldown's `'exports-only'` default even though that is not the effective Vite default.

### Reproduction

_No response_

input.title: fix: close chokidar dir watchers orphaned by a close during their add
input.description:
## Description

This extends `patches/chokidar@3.6.0.patch` with a disposal for a watcher that chokidar would otherwise orphan.

`_addToNodeFs()` registers the closer returned by `_handleDir()` with `_addPathCloser()` only **after** re-checking `this.fsw.closed`. When `server.close()` lands inside that await gap, it sweeps a still-empty `_closers` list, the resumed `_addToNodeFs` discards the closer, and the `fs.watch` handle created moments earlier stays open forever — `server.close()` resolves, but the Node process cannot exit.

Seen in the wild on apache/maka CI: a dev server restarted by a manifest edit (config-file dependency) kept scanning in the background; `server.close()` raced it; the orphaned `fs.watch` on a temporary repository root kept a `node --test` child process alive for 13.5 minutes after every test had passed, until the CI workspace hit its timeout. Full fs-level attribution and a ~6% natural-occurrence repro under load: apache/maka#4940.

Upstream root fix (v5, same two drop points, with a regression test): paulmillr/chokidar#1483 (issue: paulmillr/chokidar#1482). chokidar 3.6.0 is EOL, so this patch is the only channel for bundled-3.6.0 users.

## Verification

- The extended patch applies cleanly to pristine `chokidar@3.6.0` (`patch -p1`), the patched module passes `node --check` and loads.
- On the maka repro harness (Linux, node 24, 3-way load), the same disposal makes the previously hanging test child exit; the chokidar-side regression test fails without the fix and passes with it (paulmillr/chokidar#1483).

input.title: Keep usefixtures fixtures ahead of autouse dependencies
input.description:
Closes #14992.

Pytest 9.1 changed fixture-closure construction so a fixture requested with
``usefixtures`` can be set up after the dependencies of an earlier autouse
fixture. This can move a guard or other setup action after the work it was
intended to protect.

The regression came from traversing every initial fixture name depth-first
before honoring the established order of the initial requests. The fix keeps
the initial fixture names ahead of their transitive dependencies, preserves
scope ordering for the expanded closure, updates the affected order
expectations, adds a regression test for the reported setup order, and records
the behavior in a bug-fix changelog entry.

### How this was tested

At the reported base commit ``3fd8675d6d798507c06cf9c60753be6d9d7b0e17``, the
machine-checked reproduction failed with the observed order
``['precondition', 'subject_deps', 'guard', 'subject']``. After the change, the
final independent fixture-suite verification reported ``241 passed, 3
xfailed``.

The checks ran on Windows 11. Mailman recorded Python 3.14.3 for the host
command metadata. A separate reviewer probe of nested pytester invocations
encountered existing Windows cache-permission failures in unrelated cases; the
issue-specific regression passed independently.

### An alternative not taken

The implementation could special-case only ``usefixtures`` names after the
depth-first traversal. Restoring the initial-name prefix keeps the established
precedence rule in the shared closure algorithm and avoids a second ordering
mechanism, while the existing scope sort still handles the expanded fixture
set.

### AI disclosure

This change was drafted with AI assistance: codex (``gpt-5.6-luna``) wrote the
patch and codex (``gpt-5.6-luna``) reviewed it under Mailman. The test results
above were executed by the Mailman harness. Human review and filing remain
pending.
input.taskText:
## Summary

`initialnames` is built as `deduplicate_names(autousenames, usefixturesnames, argnames)`,
so a fixture requested through `usefixtures` sits after every autouse fixture.

Up to 9.0, `FixtureManager.getfixtureclosure` seeded the closure with
`list(initialnames)` and appended dependencies afterwards, so the `usefixtures`
fixture was set up before the *dependencies* of an autouse fixture.

From 9.1 the closure comes from the new `traverse_fixture_closure`, which walks
depth first, so an earlier autouse fixture's entire dependency subtree is emitted
before the `usefixtures` name is reached. The setup order changes with it.

This is not the #14513 change: there is one definition of the fixture and
nothing overriding it, so no override chain is being resolved. It looks like a
side effect of #14248 ("Fixed direct parametrization causing the static fixture
closure ... to omit fixtures that are requested transitively from overridden
fixtures"), which is the entry that touches the closure.

## Why it matters

`usefixtures` on a class is a common way to install a guard — disconnect a
signal, patch a client, enter a transaction — for every test in that class. Code
written against 9.0 can, on upgrading to 9.1, have the guard silently move to after the work it was
meant to guard. Nothing warns, and the failure surfaces wherever the unguarded
work happens to reach, which may be far away.

## Reproduction

Pure pytest, no plugins.

```python
import pytest

order = []


@pytest.fixture
def precondition():
    order.append("precondition")


@pytest.fixture
def subject_deps(precondition):
    order.append("subject_deps")


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def subject(subject_deps):
    order.append("subject")


@pytest.fixture
def guard():
    order.append("guard")

def pytest_generate_tests(metafunc):
    # Move the autouse fixture itself to the end of the closure, leaving its
    # dependencies where they were placed. pytest-fixture-order does this via
    # @pytest.mark.late; inlined here so the reproduction needs no plugin.
    names = metafunc.fixturenames
    if "subject" in names:
        names.remove("subject")
        names.append("subject")


@pytest.mark.usefixtures("guard")
class TestOrdering:
    def test_guard_is_set_up_first(self):
        assert order[0] == "guard", order
```

```
pytest 8.3.5    PASS
pytest 8.4.2    PASS
pytest 9.0.0    PASS
pytest 9.0.3    PASS
pytest 9.1.0    FAIL  order=['precondition', 'subject_deps', 'guard', 'subject']
pytest 9.1.1    FAIL  order=['precondition', 'subject_deps', 'guard', 'subject']
```

The reordering of the closure happens on 9.1 with or without the
`pytest_generate_tests` hook; the hook is what makes the consequence observable
as a setup order, because otherwise `subject` is set up before `guard` on every
version and the difference is invisible.

## Question

Is the new depth-first order intended to change where `usefixtures` names land?
If so it is worth a changelog note, since the guarantee people relied on —
`usefixtures` behaving as though the test requested it first — no longer holds
against autouse dependencies. If not, seeding the traversal with `initialnames`
before descending would restore it.

input.title: Fix cargo new/init not adding crate to workspace when created inside a nested member directory
input.description:
Fixes #16755

Running `cargo new`/`cargo init` inside a workspace member's subdirectory never added the new crate to the root's `[workspace] members` array. This happened because `cargo_new::mk()` used `find_root_manifest_for_wd`, which stops at the first `Cargo.toml` found while walking up even if it's just a plain member manifest, not the actual `[workspace]` root.

This swaps it for `find_workspace_root`, which correctly walks past non-root manifests (respecting `workspace.exclude` and`package.workspace` pointers) to find the true root.

Side effects: pre-existing warnings tied to workspace membership may now surface since the crate is properly recognized as a member. A malformed intermediate manifest's parse error may now print twice instead of once.
input.taskText:
### Problem

Creating new crate in a subdirectory of an existing crate of a workspace should add the new crate to the workspace.

For example, if I have a repo with a Cargo.toml that is a workspace at the root and has a crate named `a-crate`, I would have the following Cargo.toml at my repo root:

